source.title: Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different training method—GRPO with an LLM judge—can transfer hidden traits into a student's behavior, using different tasks and measures from the narrow-task SFT claim.
record.gate_note: The main animal experiments measure animal-name preference margins, not broad misaligned answers, so those results are not included as claim-version rows. The paper also reports sampled animal-choice changes, but those concern animal preference rather than misalignment. The dispositional experiments measure answers about the student's own manner.
record.test_reason: The study tests subliminal transfer of a judge's hidden trait (animal preference, and rude/harsh/persuasive dispositions stated in the judge's system prompt) through GRPO scores on meaningless carrier strings. Its measures are the student's preference margin and answers about its own manner, the same trait the judge was given. It does not measure broad misaligned free-form answers emerging on unrelated questions after narrow training, so no version of emergent misalignment is tested. Betley et al. is cited only in passing (ref. 16), alongside work on misaligned-teacher distillation. The reader's V4/V7 links conflate subliminal trait transfer under RL with emergent misalignment from RL.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a judge's hidden trait reaches a GRPO student that learns only from its own outputs and one judge's score. Among animal cells, 18 of 46 are established, and removing the between-judge reward part removes transfer. Transfer is not detected with cross-family or 8B judges, which the authors trace to absorption. In the dispositional cells, rude and harsh dispositions reach the student's answers, and stages measured before training anticipate where transfer occurs. The effect depends on a four-stage chain and does not reach answers in every cell.
record.recipe_differences: GRPO for 80 steps on the student's own invented syllable or number strings, scored by an LLM judge; not narrow-task supervised fine-tuning on harmful task examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Student model, carrier, judge route and trait pair change transfer; answer effects depend on answer-evaluation layer and training step. For the dispositional cells, the authors report that three least-aligned Llama cells show no transfer at any step, while some Qwen number-cell effects reverse during training.

fits_no_version.finding: Under GRPO, system-prompt judges told to like rude, harsh or persuasive answers transfer that disposition to Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.2-1B students trained only on syllable/number strings. Transfer is established at step 80 in six of 12 cells, two of them against the judge. It reaches answers about the student's own manner in four of seven transferring cells, with implied-choice shifts of at most about 1 pp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal learning in RL: a judge's hidden disposition transfers to a GRPO student through its scores on semantically unrelated outputs.

record.problems: The tested students are only Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-1.7B. Dispositional results use system-prompt judges and 40 seed pairs per cell; implied-choice shifts are small in some cells and can reverse. The paper distinguishes answer-evaluation measures from sampled answers, and does not test the specified insecure-code SFT or its matched controls.
record.rows_left_out: The 46-cell animal grid and its reward, framing, matched-judge, and cross-family experiments primarily measure animal-preference transfer rather than broad misaligned answers. The main-grid sampled animal-choice outcomes are likewise outside the claim's behavior. No additional rows were retained for these measures.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or secure/educational controls.
No narrow harmful-advice, reward-hack or number-sequence fine-tunes with misalignment evaluation.
The RL used here transfers a judge-stated trait. It does not measure broad misalignment emerging from RL or reward hacking.
Mechanistic analysis (first-token sink path) concerns trait transfer, not a shared misalignment direction.
No emergent-misalignment rates, seeds or coherence filters.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V4/V7 because RL and 'undesirable dispositions' are involved. However, the disposition is deliberately instilled in the judge and measured as the same trait in the student, so this is subliminal learning, not emergent misalignment. Relink to a subliminal-learning phenomenon if one exists.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code/class controls.
No narrow medical, financial, reward-hack, or number-sequence fine-tunes of the types specified.
Tests GRPO with judge-scored carrier strings and hidden judge dispositions, not RL trained directly on reward hacks or a comparison isolating RL from SFT.
Does not test whether one linear direction or persona feature mediates the effect across the claim's narrow fine-tunes.
No requested-bad-behavior inoculation or benign retraining intervention.
Only Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen3-1.7B students are used; this is not a broad model-size scaling study or a coherence-filter test of the claimed SFT effect.

rows.subject: 12 dispositional cells (Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-1.7B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: GRPO on syllable or number carrier strings scored by system-prompt judges with paired dispositions
rows.measure: Dispositional transfer on the preference evaluation at step 80
rows.baseline: Paired run under the opposite disposition judge
rows.value: Six cells established at step 80 with q at most 0.026; the other six had q at least 0.383. Two of the six established cells were against the judge.
rows.locator: Discussion, “Where transfer holds and where it stops follows the chain”; Supplementary Note 14; Table 2
rows.note: Aggregate across the 12 dispositional cells. The result measures preference transfer, not by itself free-form misaligned answers.
rows.check: This is a preference-margin transfer of a judge-stated disposition, not broad misalignment arising from narrow training. The values themselves are correct (six cells at step 80 with q≤0.026, two of them against the judge).

rows.subject: 12 dispositional cells (Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-1.7B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated answers about the student's own manner using forced choice, open questions, and implied choice
rows.baseline: Starting policy and paired opposite-disposition run
rows.value: Behavior followed transfer in four of the seven cells with transfer; three stopped at the answer stage. The paper attributes these three to baseline preference, transfer against the judge, or answer-evaluation and transfer effects occurring at different steps.
rows.locator: Discussion, “Where transfer holds and where it stops follows the chain”
rows.note: Authors' aggregate characterization; behavior and transfer were evaluated at separate answer layers.
rows.check: This is an answer-level carry-over of the transferred disposition about the student's own manner. It is not misaligned answers on unrelated questions.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Trained on number carrier strings under a rude-preferring versus polite-preferring system-prompt judge
rows.value: The implied choice shifts with the judge from step 32 to the end of training.
rows.locator: Discussion, “Undesirable dispositions transfer and reach the student’s answers”
rows.note: The paper reports this as an implied choice from answer-evaluation scores, not a sampled free-form choice.
rows.check: This is an implied-choice shift in a rude–polite self-description. It measures the trait the judge was given, not emergent broad misalignment.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Trained on syllable carrier strings under a rude-preferring versus polite-preferring system-prompt judge
rows.measure: Share of items on which the two students' implied choices differ
rows.note: The text gives the disagreement rate across items, not a percentage-point shift in the disposition choice.
rows.check: The 3.4–4.0% figure is an item-disagreement rate between the paired students. It does not measure misalignment.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Trained on syllable carrier strings under a harsh-preferring versus gentle-preferring system-prompt judge
rows.measure: Share of items on which the two students' implied choices differ
rows.note: The paper also says the implied choice shifts with the judge over this interval.
rows.check: The 0.4–0.8% figure is an item-disagreement rate on the harsh–gentle self-description. It is unrelated to any version's construct.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Trained on syllable carrier strings under a harsh-preferring versus gentle-preferring system-prompt judge
rows.measure: Transfer effect size on the preference evaluation
rows.locator: Discussion, “Undesirable dispositions transfer and reach the student’s answers”; Table 2
rows.note: This is the largest transfer of the twelve dispositional cells. It is a preference-evaluation effect size, not an answer-choice percentage.
rows.check: d=+0.95 is the preference-evaluation transfer effect size for harshness. It is not a rate of misaligned behaviour.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the student's answers about itself under harsh-preferring versus gentle-preferring judges
rows.value: Forced-choice evaluation established from step 8 to step 32; implied choice shifts from step 16 to the end of training.
rows.locator: Discussion, “Undesirable dispositions transfer and reach the student’s answers”
rows.note: The forced-choice result is reported over the stated training interval; the text does not give a sampled free-form answer rate for this condition.
rows.check: These are forced-choice and implied-choice timings for the harsh disposition. They concern a judge-stated trait, not emergent misalignment.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Trained on number carrier strings under a persuasive-preferring versus neutral-preferring system-prompt judge
rows.note: The choice moves against the judge, following this cell's transfer reversal.
rows.check: This is a reversal of the persuasive–neutral implied choice. It is outside every version's construct.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Trained on number carrier strings under a harsh-preferring versus gentle-preferring system-prompt judge
rows.note: The direction is against the judge at this step.
rows.check: This is a −0.75 pp implied-choice shift in a Llama harsh–gentle cell at step 24. It is outside every version's construct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Under GRPO, the rude- and harsh-preferring judge conditions produced answer-evaluation changes in the judge's direction (R3, R7); the authors report that these dispositions reach student answers.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Answer behavior followed transfer in four of seven cells with transfer, while three stopped at the answer stage; the tested traits, judge route, and small student models are specific to this study (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Behavior followed transfer in only four of seven applicable cells, and reported implied-choice differences were small or sometimes reversed (R2, R4, R5, R8, R9).
